summary:
Sections 153, 154 and 155 of Tuvalu's Penal Code make male homosexual intercourse, attempts to commit it, and gross indecency between males felonies carrying up to 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively. ILGA World's jurisdiction database records the offence as in force and dates the provisions to the colonial era. The exposure is gendered: because the provisions define conduct by male persons, a transgender woman read by police as male falls within them.

The evidence on enforcement is thin and old. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tuvalu describes criminalisation under the Penal Code with no prosecutions of consenting adults recorded, and reports no government abuses of LGBT people in that year. The same assessment attributes discrimination to traditional customs that perpetuate religious and social prejudice rather than to state action. Nothing in the inventory documents a conviction under these sections at any date, and nothing more recent than 2013 on enforcement practice is available here.

No detention-condition, strip-search or custody-treatment findings for transgender detainees appear anywhere in the sourced material. The inventory also contains no hate-crime incidents, hate-crime statistics or hate-crime legislation for Tuvalu, and no entry, visa or border-screening rules with any bearing on gender marker or trans status.

On the protective side, Tuvalu was among roughly 80 signatory states to the UN joint statement on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011, recalling General Assembly resolutions on the subject. The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, alongside gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Constitutional protection is narrower: the freedom from discrimination in section 27 of the Constitution, as amended in 2023, lists sex but does not refer to sexual orientation, and no gender-identity or gender-expression protection is described in any source.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. The 2023 constitutional amendments prohibited same-sex marriage, and section 43(2)(b) of the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities defines a family unit as a marriage between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others. The Marriage Act (Cap 29) does not expressly bar recognition of same-sex unions but assumes parties are male and female, and same-sex marriages do not appear in its restrictions on marriage; no partner-visa, next-of-kin or foreign-union recognition provisions are discussed in the sources.

The Penal Code's asymmetry matters for anyone assessing personal exposure: the age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal intercourse and for lesbian sex, while the male homosexual provisions carry separate felony penalties regardless of that threshold, an arrangement that affects young men who have sex with men. A 2005 study found about 14 per cent of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 had had sex with a male partner at some point.
tangentialFactors:
The neighbouring comparison available in the inventory is one of process rather than outcome: Tuvalu's 2011 signature on the UN joint statement placed it alongside roughly 80 states documenting a diplomatic position on sexual orientation and gender identity, while its own Penal Code retained the colonial-era offences. The sources do not show how that position was followed up in domestic policy.

The country's health machinery is the one area where gender-diverse populations are named explicitly in an official document. The Tuvalu Ministry of Health's 2017 Global AIDS Progress Report sets out the national HIV response and draws on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations, a regional exercise covering men who have sex with men and transgender Tuvaluans. That is a state acknowledgment of these populations in a health context, which sits alongside the absence of gender-identity protection in the Constitution.

Scale shapes what can be observed. UNAIDS estimates for 2017 put the national population of men who have sex with men at about 300 and of pinapinaaine at about 40, so enforcement patterns, service coverage and incident reporting would be difficult to detect even if they existed.

Health services for key populations operate through the national HIV response described in the Ministry of Health's 2017 Global AIDS Progress Report, which builds on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study covering men who have sex with men and transgender Tuvaluans. National estimates for 2017 suggest about 300 MSM and about 40 pinapinaaine. No education-policy, school-bullying or youth-service findings are supplied by the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement evidence stops in 2013. The inventory contains no human rights report, court record or police data for Tuvalu after that year, so whether the Penal Code sections remain unprosecuted is unresolved rather than confirmed.

No entry, visa, passport or border-screening rules are sourced for Tuvalu, including any requirement to declare or disclose gender history on arrival. Absence of such rules in this inventory is not evidence that none exist.

Treatment of transgender detainees is unsourced: the material contains no detention conditions, strip-search practice, placement decisions or complaints data for trans people in custody. Likewise, no hate-crime legislation or incident record is available for Tuvalu, so the presence or absence of a hate-crime regime is unresolved.

The inventory does not state how a gender marker change on a passport or birth certificate is handled in Tuvalu, whether any legal recognition of gender identity exists, or how foreign same-sex marriages are treated by the Marriage Act. No source documents consular or immigration consequences of the 2023 constitutional amendment for foreign visitors.
